title: Per-token response waterfall — experimentation & grooming notes
body:
Context:
This doc captures early UX brainstorming, lightweight wireframe descriptions, and a short backlog groom for a per-token response waterfall view in the Console. The goal is to help engineers and product owners quickly surface which tokens (or token groups) drive cost and latency for a given model invocation stream. Think of it as a hybrid between a network waterfall and a flamegraph but token-aware and aligned to invocation roles (system, user, model, function outputs).

Why we need it (short):
- Current token-cost dashboards show aggregates (per-invocation, per-route) but hide where cost/latency accumulates inside long responses.
- Teams need an easy way to find hotspots: repeated prompt prefixes, heavy sampling tails, long function call outputs, and unexpected model stalls (KV cache thrash).
- This view should enable quick remediation actions: change batching, change quantization profile, pin a model, or add prefix caching.

Primary goals for the first iteration:
1) Make per-invocation token timing and token-cost visible with minimal noise.
2) Allow pivoting between token timeline (waterfall) and token histogram (cost/latency grouped).
3) Provide actionable recommendations directly from the view (one-click suggestions that generate a runbook link or PR template).

Target audience:
- ML infra engineers diagnosing slow tails or throughput regressions.
- Product engineers optimizing unit economics of text-heavy endpoints.
- Solutions/SEs preparing recommendations for customers on Dedicated/Private plans.

Hypotheses to test:
- H1: Visualizing token-level latency as a waterfall will make it 3x faster for an engineer to identify if the latency is model compute vs. pre/post-processing.
- H2: Grouping tokens by semantic role (system/user/function/model) reduces the time to identify unintentional prompt repetition by at least 40%.
- H3: Auto-suggested fixes based on detected patterns (e.g., long function output -> recommend streaming) will be adopted for 20%+ of identified incidents in pilot customers.

Wireframe sketches (described in prose for quick iteration):
- Layout A (left-heavy): Left column: invocation metadata (model, version, region, route, request-id, timestamp, cost estimate). Center: horizontal waterfall timeline where each token is a small stripe whose width = time spent for that token. Colors by role (system=purple, user=blue, model=green, function=orange). Hover shows token text, token index, cum-latency, compute vs. IO breakdown. Right column: token histogram and top-3 suggested actions.
- Layout B (compact): Top strip: mini-timeline slider for long responses. Main area: stacked bands representing groups of tokens (prefix, body, generation tail). Each band has stacked bars representing per-token time; clicking a band expands to granular tokens. Inline sparklines show token cost trend vs. baseline.
- Layout C (trace-first): Integrate with existing invocation traces. When a trace is open, overlay token waterfall aligned to trace events (e.g., batching boundary, cache miss). This makes it easy to see correlation between infra events and token stalls.

Interactions and microflows:
- Hover on token: tooltip shows raw token text (truncated to safe preview), token id, per-token cost estimate (token-cost model), latency split (model compute vs. network/serialization), source (prompt/stop/func).
- Click token: open right rail with context: surrounding 20 tokens, prompt references (Jira/PR if exists), suggested experiments (reduce max_new_tokens, enable prefix caching, change sampling).
- Time-slice selection: drag to select a range; the system can run a simulated re-cost with suggested optimizations (fast, locally simulated) and show delta in tokens and milliseconds.
- Compare mode: pick two invocations (A vs B) and render token alignment — highlights token-level diffs (repeats, hallucinated function outputs).

Data model assumptions and mock data sample (for prototyping):
- Input: invocation id, sequence of tokens [{token_text, token_index, role, latency_ms, compute_ms, io_ms, bytes}].
- Derived: cumulative_latency, per_token_cost_usd (using per-token pricing model), causal_grouping (prefix/body/tail).
- Small mock row example (text):
  invocation: inv-20260215-abc
  tokens: "System: You are an assistant<|0|>" (role=system, latency=2ms)
  "User: Summarize quarterly results<|1|>" (role=user, latency=3ms)
  "Model: The revenue grew by 18%...<|2|>" (role=model, latency sequence: first tokens 6ms, long token around 120ms at token_index 87)

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- The waterfall renders for invocations up to 4k tokens with UI virtualization, and remains interactive (<200ms hover response).
- Hover/click reveals token-level cost and latency breakdown (compute vs IO) for at least 95% of tokens in sample datasets.
- One-click action that opens a prepopulated runbook/PR template for the top suggestion.

Backlog / grooming items (prioritized):
- [P0] Data pipe: expose per-token latency/cost in invocation events stream (ENG-Trace team) — JIRA-RT-789.
- [P0] UI virtualized token row rendering component (DEV-UI) — block until data pipe available.
- [P1] Proposal for safe token preview (PII heuristics + redact policy) — SOC-23.
- [P1] Auto-suggestion rules engine (simple ruleset first: repeated prefix, long function output, high tail latency) — implement prototype in Node for quick testing.
- [P2] Compare mode: two-invocation alignment UX and delta highlighting.
- [P2] Export snapshots (PNG + JSON) for incident reports.
- [P3] Integrate with rollouts: surface which model version served each token, show pinned vs fallback behavior.

Open questions / risks:
- Privacy: showing raw token text could expose PII. We need a masking policy and an audit trail for who viewed raw tokens. Feels like a blocker for enterprise/private until policy in place.
- Cost accuracy: token cost is a derived estimate because different models/quantization change per-token compute. Make it clear these are estimates and show confidence band.
- Performance: rendering many small DOM elements for tokens is risky. Prefer Canvas or WebGL virtualization for the waterfall.
- Sampling vs full capture: capturing every token for all invocations is high-volume. We should sample for high-frequency endpoints and always keep full captures for slow/failed invocations.

Quick experiments to run (week-by-week):
- Week 1: lightweight mockup with synthetic traces (Canvas timeline), internal usability with infra and serving teams (goal: 3 sessions).
- Week 2: wire up to real sampled invocation data for 3 beta routes, validate data model and latency splits.
- Week 3: pilot auto-suggestion rules and record adoption metrics over 2 weeks.

Notes to reviewers (what I want feedback on):
- Is the left/center/right layout more useful than a compact banded layout for triage?
- How strict do we need to be about storing raw token text? Would redaction-by-default + unlock-on-need suffice?
- Which suggestions feel like low-friction vs. dangerous (e.g., recommending quantization changes should probably not be in-console without guardrails).

Next steps (short):
1) Schedule a 45m sketch review with infra (Marco), serving-runtime (Diego) and SOC (Ruth) — propose Tue 2026-03-02.
2) Spin up a quick Canvas prototype (UI) and a small synthetic trace generator (Dev-UI) by 2026-03-09.
3) Create JIRA epic for data pipeline changes and mark P0 items.
